_comment: Universal SAP knowledge. Nothing in this file is customer-specific -- it is true of
any SAP system, so it ships with the skill and is NOT part of a site config.
A site config may override any dict entry per key, and appends to list-valued
entries unless it sets "replace": true. See references/configuration.md.
_comment_non_discriminating: Tables every module reads all day, so a READ of one proves nothing about ownership.
Listing a table here removes it from the read/write rules -- and only from those.
A table may appear BOTH here and under a module in std_tables, which is not a
contradiction: it says 'reading KNA1 tells you nothing, but a structure NAMED after
KNA1 is customer master'. The name rules (R13/R14) resolve through the unfiltered
map for exactly that reason. LFA1 earned its place here by measurement: it was the
sole reason objects got called FI, and demoting it left held-out accuracy essentially
_comment_std_call_ignore: Framework plumbing. LSVIM* is the single most-called standard target in a typical
estate (SM30 table maintenance); left in, it misclassifies the function group of
_comment_badi_spots: R3: the STANDARD object being enhanced names the module with certainty. Keys are
matched as a prefix of, or a substring in, the BAdI spot / classic exit /
_comment_exit_includes: R4: classic SMOD exit includes (ZX<fgrp>U01 style). The include name is derived
from the SAP exit function group, so it self-classifies with certainty.
_comment_appl: R8 only, WEAK. TRDIR-APPL, the SAP application area of a program. Present on
only part of the programs. 'R' (cross-application) and '*' are deliberately
unmapped. Verify against your own estate before trusting it -- it fires last and
only when every other rule came up empty.
_comment_third_party: Open-source ABAP that ships inside customer packages. It is not custom business
code and must never occupy rows in the deliverable: abap2xlsx alone is ~330
objects and puts 78 UNCLASSIFIED ZCL_EXCEL* classes on sheet 1.

demote_reasons.AQBG: SAP Query user group (authorisation grouping, not code)
demote_reasons.ENHC: enhancement composite; its implementations carry the rows

_comment_fold_edges: Edge kinds meaning 'the target is part of my implementation', so it may be folded
into the unit. Everything else (ENHANCES_*, PARAM_CALLS_TCODE at another custom
T-Code) points at a peer or at standard SAP and must not absorb it.
_comment_evidence_mute: Edges strong enough to prove an object EXISTS in a unit, too weak to say who OWNS
the unit. `TYPE zsome_struct` is the clearest case: declaring a structure that
happens to live in the MM package does not make the program MM. Including these in
the module evidence pushes multi-module attribution up -- straight
_comment_std_name_wrappers: Custom names that WRAP a standard SAP name: transaction and screen variants,
parameterised T-Codes, forms named after the standard program they print for, and
BW extractor enhancements named after the DataSource they extend. Without this rule
variants are the largest unclassifiable population in an estate that customises
standard transactions instead of writing new ones -- most variants and many
parameterised T-Codes have no other signal at all.
Transaction patterns are ANCHORED and every one requires a digit or a distinctive
letter run, because an unanchored 'ME' or 'CO' would match half of any estate. The
DataSource patterns are deliberately NOT anchored: the token sits mid-name
(ZXX_BW_0FI_GL_4) and '0FI_' or '2LIS_02_' cannot be mistaken for anything else.
_comment_webi: WEBI = Web Service Definition. Its <VEPFUNCTION> blocks name the function modules it
exposes (<FUNCTION> + <IS_EXPOSED>X). Those FMs -- and the module that owns them --
are what the service actually does, so the edge to their function group is the only
sound way to attribute a web service. Attributing it by its own name attributes a
_comment_external_comm: Markers that the code talks to something OUTSIDE the SAP system. Not module
evidence -- an outbound HTTP call says nothing about SD or MM -- but a first-class
fact about the object: it is part of the integration surface, and the integration
team has a stake in it. Fed to the configured modules.integration_bucket by R11.
CALL FUNCTION ... DESTINATION is outbound RFC; EXEC SQL and the ADBC classes are
external_comm_markers: native SQL to an external database
_comment_special_modules: Universal SAP knowledge sometimes lands on a concern that is NOT an SAP module:
an IDoc segment is integration, a logon exit is Basis. The skill must not invent a
bucket name for a customer, so entries below may use the tokens '@INTEGRATION' and
'@TECHNICAL'. They resolve to modules.integration_bucket and modules.technical_bucket
from the site config, and a rule whose token has no bucket configured simply does
not fire -- it never falls back to a core module it cannot justify.
_comment_infotype: SAP generates a fixed DDIC family per HR infotype: P9000 (record), PA9000
(transparent table), PS9000 (field structure), P9000_AF (query fields), plus a
screen structure. None of the names carries a module token and none is referenced
from custom code -- the HR framework dispatches infotype screens from T777D -- so a
single custom infotype leaves ten-plus objects unattributed while being
unambiguously HR. The four-digit number in the customer range is what makes the
_comment_append: An append structure has no business words of its own -- ZZMC11VA1ITM, CI_BSIS,
ZBW_CE3XXXX -- but it always names its base, and the base IS the module. SAP's own
generated short text states it outright ('Append for MC11VA1ITM', 'Fields from
BSEG', 'View on MARD'), which is why the text patterns matter as much as the name.
_comment_std_object_prefixes: Standard DDIC families whose NAME states the module, for resolving what a custom
object appends to or extends. Kept deliberately short: every entry is a fixed SAP
naming family, not a guess from letters. CE1-CE4 are the CO-PA line-item and segment
tables; MC<nn> are LIS communication structures where <nn> is the LIS application
(02 purchasing, 03 inventory controlling, 04 shop floor, 05 QM, 06 PM, 11 SIS sales,
12 SIS shipping, 13 SIS billing); T*KE/KED are CO-PA customizing; WPU/WPD are the
retail POS interface and WBB the bonus-buy/listing download.
_comment_idoc: IDoc naming is the most discriminating content signal an IDoc-heavy estate has, and it
is invisible to the table rules: a segment type is a DDIC structure, not a table, so
'ls_seg TYPE e1kna1m' reads as nothing at all. Both halves of the fact are worth
keeping -- ZE1KNA1M is an interface object AND a customer-master object -- so the
rule ticks the integration bucket and the module of what the segment extends.
Message types are even better: 'pi_mestyp = WBBDLD' names the business process.
_comment_composition: Edges that mean 'the target is PART OF the source', as opposed to 'the source calls
the target'. A DDIC leaf holds no code, so these are the only facts it has: without
them every data element, domain and table type has zero inbound references and lands
in Unattached labelled 'attributed via its consumer' while having no recorded
consumer at all. They are used by the residual pass to give a component the module
of whatever uses it -- NOT as fold edges, because a domain is not part of a
program's entry-point closure and must not become a member row.
_comment_container_types: Types that OWN their members rather than being owned by them: an enhancement
composite is the union of its implementations, a Query user group the union of its
queries. They inherit downward, from children, and never get a row of their own.
_comment_fugr_include: A function group's includes are named L<AREA>TOP / L<AREA>UXX / L<AREA>F01 and a
copy of a standard group keeps that shape with a Z in front: ZLKED2TOP is the TOP
include of a clone of SAP's KED2 (CO-PA planning). Such an include has no
declarations a table rule can read and no inbound edge, so it is unattributable by
everything else -- but its own name states the standard function group it belongs to.
_comment_std_data_elements: The strongest signal a fieldless-looking structure has. A custom table's short text
may be its own name and its check tables may all be non-discriminating, but the data
elements its fields are typed with are chosen from SAP's dictionary and they name the
business object: PAE_SNAMT is a payroll amount, GKONT_LTXT is the
offsetting G/L account, TPLST is a transportation planning point. Matched
Deliberately excluded: MANDT, WERKS, LGORT, MATNR-style keys that every module uses.
Those live in non_discriminating_data_elements and are skipped, for the same reason
MARA is skipped in the table rules -- see _comment_non_discriminating.
_comment_presentation_types: A SmartStyle, a page format and a MIME logo have no business logic to read and no
name convention to match. They are formatting assets, and the honest answer is the
technical bucket with that stated as the reason -- not silence, which reads as a
failure of the index, and not a business module, which would be invented.
_comment_definitional_edges: Edges where the SOURCE is defined by the TARGET, the opposite of composition_edges.
A table type IS its row type; a table-maintenance object IS about the table it
maintains; a screen variant IS a variant of its program. So these inherit downward,
from the target, and they are tried FIRST -- 'this object is that object' is a
stronger claim than 'something that uses this object is MM'.
_comment_std_name_ignore: Standard programs and transactions that every module uses, so wrapping one says
nothing about the wrapper. SM30 maintains a table -- the module belongs to the
TABLE, not to SM30 -- and SAPLSVAR is the variant dialog, SAPLSLVC_FULLSCREEN the
ALV grid. Mapping any of them to a module would attribute twenty unrelated units to
whatever bucket the list happened to name; leaving them out of the tables entirely
would instead park them on the research worklist forever. So they are listed here:
known, and known to carry no module.
This is the R9 twin of std_call_ignore, which does the same job for function calls.
_comment_generated_names: Machine-generated program names. 'GP' followed by a long alphanumeric run is a
generated table-maintenance or print program; the name is a hash and carries no
business meaning whatsoever. Listing them here keeps them off the research worklist,
which otherwise asks a human to look up a hash on every single run.
